sections.overview: The puma, also called cougar or mountain lion, is a large cat native to the Americas. Usually solitary, it ranges from western Canada through much of South America. Its presence across varied landscapes makes it one of the continent’s most widely distributed native mammals.
sections.identification: Adults have a tawny, grey-brown or reddish coat, usually paler underneath, with a small head, rounded ears, powerful hindquarters and a long, thick tail. Adults lack spots; kittens are spotted, and their markings fade as they grow. Size varies across this species’ wide range. A North American reference gives adult males a total length of about 2.0–2.4 m and a usual mass of 53–100 kg (average about 62 kg); females average about 2.05 m and usually weigh 29–64 kg (average about 42 kg). Shoulder height is reported at about 60–76 cm. No reliable general body-width measurement was found.
sections.habitat: Pumas occupy forests, scrub, grasslands, deserts and wetlands, from lowlands to mountains. They use places with prey and cover, including dense vegetation, rocky crevices and caves. Habitat use varies locally: Florida panthers, for example, use swamp forest and wooded hammocks.
sections.diet: This carnivore takes locally available prey. Deer are important across much of North America; elk, moose, wild pigs, guanacos, hares and smaller mammals may also be eaten. Pumas stalk and ambush prey, then cover large carcasses to return for later meals.
sections.behavior: Adults generally live alone, except during mating and while females raise young. Home ranges can overlap; a male’s range may encompass several females. Scent marks, scraped ground and scratched logs signal occupancy. Pumas may be active by day or night, often around dusk and dawn.
sections.reproduction: Pumas breed year-round, though some populations have seasonal peaks. After about three months, a female gives birth to one to six kittens in a den. Spotted at birth, they eat meat at six weeks and stay with her for about a year.
sections.ecology: As a large predator, the puma hunts herbivores and can affect where prey feed and move. Its effects depend on local conditions and interactions with other predators. Yellowstone research examines cougars alongside wolves, bears and elk; carcasses also provide food for scavengers.
sections.conservation: The IUCN assessment published in 2015 classified the species as Least Concern, while noting uncertainty and suspected declines in parts of Central and South America. Habitat loss, fragmentation, persecution, hunting and depleted prey threaten some populations. Connected habitat and reduced conflict are conservation priorities.
